Warning 14.1: Caveats for hand texturing





Since hand texturing is a sense-dependent process that involves manipulating the whole fine fraction, accurate estimation of particle size can be hampered by competing factors. Some of the more well known (Salley et al. 2018) are as follows.

Grading: a small amount of coarse sand in a finer matrix can cause underestimation of clay content because the large particles are more noticeable.
Clay mineralogy: the physical properties of 2:1 phyllosilicate clays such as smectite make it easier to form a ball or ribbon than 1:1 phyllosilicates such as kaolinite, or clay-size secondary minerals such as allophane. As a result, clay content can be underestimated in older soils weathered under humid conditions, and in volcanic ash soils.
Microstructure: in some soils, very small aggregates cannot be broken down by hand manipulation, or at best require dedicated working for over 10 minutes per sample. This characteristic can lead to clay content underestimation; but, crucially, hand texture may more closely align with in situ physical properties than laboratory texture from chemically dispersed samples.
Organic matter: organic matter can lend a spongy or silky feel to a sample, which may lead to overestimating silt and underestimating clay.
Sharpness: angular particles are more likely to be interpreted as sandy than silty.
Experience and environment: workers who spend most of their time in landscapes that have a narrow range of soil textures become more sensitive to minor variations in hand-feel, and are more likely to assign unusual textures to a different texture class even when the difference is not sufficient to justify it.

All of these confounding factors can be minimised with regular training, using a wide variety of samples of known composition.

title: 14  Texture
text:
14.3 Recording soil texture
To rapidly assess texture:

for the fine-earth fraction use one of the texture group codes in Table 14.2 per horizon
where rock fragments need to be recorded use the dominant rock fragment code in Table 14.6
where organic materials need to be recorded use one of the options in Table 14.9
do not use any further modifiers.

For routine assessment record one of the texture class codes in Table 14.13 per horizon. Where further detail is required, apply the relevant modifiers, as described in Section 14.1.
For example: for a coarse sandy loam with fine gravel: for rapid use: L(G), for routine use : KSL(FG).

title: 14  Texture
text:
14.4 Recording particle size distribution
Numerical estimates of particle size distribution for the fine-earth fraction may be desired, particularly where it is known that laboratory particle size measurements will not be available. Record field estimates of clay and sand content derived from hand texturing to the nearest 1%, and work silt out by the difference. It is recommended to add a separate error estimate (± x%) as an expression of confidence.
For example: use KLS, 70 ± 5% sand, 3% clay for a coarse loamy sand.






Note 14.7: Comparing field and laboratory assessment of texture





Both field and laboratory measurements provide useful, but distinct, information on soil particle size distribution, and the two must never be treated as interchangeable. Field-estimated and laboratory-determined values must be stored separately in databases, and one must not override the other. Laboratory particle size analysis should not be used to change field texture codes; instead, a separate ‘laboratory texture’ should be generated from the analytical results. The origin of particle size estimates must always be clearly documented.
As discussed in Warning 14.1, fine-earth texture estimated by hand in the field can include information about other soil characteristics. Estimating particle size from hand texturing requires practice and the ability to identify and account for these sources of interference.
Laboratory particle size measurement also has its limitations. Available methods can incorporate particle shape and mineralogy, but these methods are labour-intensive and generally confined to research contexts. High-throughput analyses are far more common and usually involve the removal of organic materials and soluble minerals, along with more aggressive aggregate dispersion using shaking and chemical solutions.
Below approximately 0.04 mm the method of measurement switches from sieving to less direct observations (commonly based on settling time in a liquid column). The calculations used to translate these observations into particle size estimates make some assumptions about shape and mineralogy that may not hold true for the sample under examination (see Loveland and Whalley (2001), for a more detailed discussion).




14.4.1 Recording whole-soil particle size estimates
Percentage estimates of particle size require some adjustment when reporting on a whole-soil basis. Total fine earth is the sum of the mineral fine earth and the organic matter. Clay, silt, and sand percentage estimates are initially reported as a fraction of the mineral fine earth only, and organic matter as a fraction of the total fine earth. Rock fragments are reported as a percentage of the whole soil volume.
For a worked example, take a soil with 25% clay, 35% silt, 40% sand, 15% organic matter, and 15% cobble.

The total coarse fraction is 15% of the soil volume.
The total fine fraction is 85% of the soil volume (\(100 - coarse fraction\)).
The organic fraction of the fine earth is then \(15\% \times 8.5\% = 12.75\%\).
This leaves the mineral fraction of the fine earth as \(85\% - 12.75\% = 72.25\%\).
Distributed between clay, sand and silt:

clay: \(25\% \times 72.25\% = 18.06\%\)
silt: \(35\% \times 72.25\% = 25.29\%\)
sand: \(40\% \times 72.25\% = 28.90\%\)


The final whole-earth composition is 18% clay, 25% silt, 29% sand, 15% cobble, and 13% organic matter. Report the final results in whole percentages; the method in use here can’t support any higher precision.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
15.1 Concentrations
Weathering features are distinct bodies formed within the soil through pedogenic (natural soil-forming) processes. They contain a higher amount of a particular substance (or association of substances) and thus contrast with the surrounding material. Many of these features create barriers to water movement or alter chemistry in a way that affects soil organisms and plant root growth.
Concentrations are secondary features that are not associated with specific surfaces within the soil (i.e. they do not form coatings on peds or void spaces, but rather permeate the soil mass; compare with coatings, Section 15.2). Some concentrations contrast sharply with the surrounding soil material due to differences in colour, hardness, or composition, while others may be more subtle.
For rapid assessment, record the concentration type and abundance percentage using Table 15.2. For a routine assessment, add form. For a detailed description, add size range in millimetres. Colour is not required because it is usually determined by type and may have already been recorded as a colour pattern (Section 13.3). Abundance and size can be classified using Table D.5 and Table D.8 respectively.
For example: use F NO 10% 6-8 mm for scattered small ironstone nodules.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
Note 15.1: Lamellae and laminae





Lamellae are thin bands of concentrated but uncemented soil materials, formed by pedological processes. They are usually of a finer texture than their surrounds, and may also have relatively high levels of other weathering products, such as iron precipitates or organic matter. While their formation mechanisms are still not fully understood, the presence of lamellae in a profile can signify the absence of some processes (e.g. bioturbation) and presence of others (e.g. seasonal freeze-thaw activity). Lamellae usually occur horizontally or parallel to the land surface at a scale of several metres, but can exhibit a wavy character at the sub-metre scale.
Lamellae may technically qualify as distinct soil horizons. If a single lamella is evident between two contrasting horizons, it must be described as a separate horizon rather than as a concentration. Where lamellae occur within a larger band of soil material that has consistent composition, they can be described as concentrations.
For example: use LM L 10% 3-5 mm for a series of thin clay bands observed in a larger sandy layer.
For a more detailed discussion of lamellae, see Dijkerman et al. (1967), Rawling (2000), and Bockheim and Hartemink (2013).
By contrast, laminae are thin bands of unconsolidated material with contrasting texture that have been emplaced by water, wind, or pyroclastic activity and have yet to be significantly disturbed by profile development. These geogenic layers are not weathering features and are described using terminology from Section 12.5.3. No minimum or maximum thickness requirements are specified for individual lamina due to lack of data, but anecdotally they tend to be less than 5 cm thick.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
15.2 Coatings
Coatings are layers of material that form on the surfaces of other soil features (e.g. grains, peds, or the walls of voids). Some coatings are formed by chemical precipitation, similar to concentrations, while others form as a result of selective removal processes, where the material left behind accumulates. Some coatings may be biological in origin (e.g. some ant species line their burrow tunnel walls with fine material).
For rapid assessment of coatings, record the type of the most well-developed coating using one of the options in Table 15.3. For a routine assessment include its abundance as percentage of soil surfaces covered, and its colour using the short codes in Table 13.6. For detailed assessment record all coatings observed, their respective abundances, and their colours using Munsell colour notation.
For example: use OG D 80% for well-developed, dark-coloured organic coats covering most ped surfaces.




Table 15.3: Types of surface coating














Code
Name
Description




CC
Clay coats
Appear to have more clay than the soil matrix; they are often different in colour from the adjacent matrix and are usually recognisable in sandy or loamy soils, but can be difficult to recognise in clayey soils.


ZC
Silt coats
Silt grains concentrated at surfaces; they may be residual concentrations resulting from clay removal, or may have moved in from horizons above.


SC
Sand coats
Sand grains concentrated at surfaces; they may be residual concentrations resulting from silt and/or clay removal, or may have moved in from horizons above


OG
Organic coats
Surface features that have a moist colour value of 4 or less and are rich in organic matter compared to the interior of the solid.


SQ
Sesquioxide coats
Films of sesquioxides on interfaces or impregnating interfaces. They vary in colour depending on the composition and degree of oxidation and hydration. They are difficult to identify chemically, and the different kinds cannot normally be distinguished in the field. Ferri-manganiferous coats, however, are normally very dark brown or black and effervesce vigorously with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2).


MN

Dark to black coatings of precipitated manganese oxides, reactive to H2O2.

Precipitated CaCO3. Usually pale-coloured, and reactive to HCl.


SI

Precipitated silica (SiO2). Usually pale-coloured, and non-reactive to HCl.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
15.3 Pans
Pans form when particular chemical compounds precipitate out of the soil solution and cement a layer of mineral particles (perhaps as a further accumulation and joining together of coatings and/or concentrations), or when particular particle size distributions and/or shape range become very tightly packed. Many pans are diagnostic in the New Zealand Soil Classification because they can form a barrier to plant root growth or water movement (see also Section 19.3).
For rapid assessment, record pan type using Table 15.4.
For example: use X for a fragipan.
Only record pans that are strongly developed enough to be classification-relevant. A classification-relevant pan is one that is developed enough to meet all of the relevant diagnostic requirements listed in the New Zealand Soil Classification. Many (but not all) pans have dedicated conventional horizon names. The full definitions of those horizons are available in Chapter 18.
For routine assessment, add continuity (Table 15.5) and structure (Table 15.6).
For example: use FBS for a vesicular iron-pan that has been broken up by deep ripping.
Pans can optionally be described in detail in terms of type, thickness, continuity, structure, strength and cementation. Pans comprise distinct horizons, so their thickness is defined using horizon boundaries. Their strength and cementation are assessed using Table 16.2 and Table 16.10. Codes for type, continuity and structure are given below. Note that continuity can only be observed in large pits or exposures.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
15.4 Stress features
Stress features develop along fissures or on ped faces in soils that shrink and swell as water content changes. Stress features are usually shiny but do not differ in colour from the soil matrix. Magnification may be required to observe them clearly. Stress features will not develop in sandy soil textures (see Table 14.2).
Stress features can be optionally recorded during a routine or detailed soil description. Describe type using Table 15.7 and abundance as the integer percentage of ped faces covered.
For example: use SL 30% in a well-developed Vertic Melanic Soil.




Table 15.7: Stress feature type














Code
Name
Description




SL
Slickensides
Smooth faces with linear grooves, formed from peds sliding past each other.


PF
Pressure faces
Smooth planar faces, formed from peds pressing against each other without sliding.

title: 15  Weathering features
text:
15.5 Cryofeatures
Cryoturbation refers to the physical disturbance and mixing of soil caused by repeated freezing and thawing. This process commonly occurs in soils exposed to seasonal or historical freeze-thaw cycles. Affected soils may show discontinuous horizon boundaries and physical mixing as a result of intense shrink-swell activity caused by ice formation.
Freezing and thawing can also accelerate downslope movement (solifluction), often incorporating angular, poorly sorted rock fragments into the soil. These features can be recognised by examining horizon boundary characteristics (Section 11.3, Section 11.4), colour patterns from mixing (Section 13.3.1), and rock fragment characteristics (Section 12.2.1).

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.1 Background
‘Consistence’ is a general term for the field-assessed behaviour of soil materials in response to applied physical stress over a range of soil-water states from wet to dry. The consistence properties described for mineral soil materials are strength, failure, fluidity, penetration resistance, packing, sensitivity, induration, plasticity, stickiness, dilatancy, and dry coherence. For organic materials, rubbed fibre content is relevant.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.1.1 Soil-water content
Some consistence properties (strength, failure, penetration resistance) vary markedly with soil-water content. The soil moisture status of the material should therefore be recorded at the time of description (see Section 11.6) . Consistence descriptions of the same soils at different moisture states allow the change in consistence with moisture to be described. Other consistence properties are described at reference water contents.


16.1.2 Sampling for consistence tests
Consistence tests should be performed down-profile, with at least one sample tested per horizon. Samples should be taken from the mid-point of each horizon. Additional samples in transition zones may also be of interest. For most of these tests, a 30 mm sample cube of soil (27 cm3) must be carefully extracted, preferably with a sharp knife. Keeping the sample size and shape consistent helps produce consistent results. Tests that involve remoulding the soil may use smaller volumes, but must use no less than ~3 cm3 (a 15 mm cube).
Within each horizon the consistence tests that can and should be undertaken will depend on the cohesion (Section 16.2) of the soil materials in that horizon. Table 16.1 illustrates which tests are appropriate for different soil materials.

Note 16.1: Consistence tests and the New Zealand Soil Classification





For classifying using the New Zealand Soil Classification, particular tests down to or at a certain depth may be required to progress through the ‘Key to Soil Orders’. At the soil order level, these are as follows.

Gley Soils: must not have any moderately or very fluid (Section 16.11) layers within 30 cm of the soil surface. Unconfined soil strength (Section 16.3.1) and cementation (Section 16.12) tests may be required to confirm absence of an underlying fragipan.
Ultic Soils: need an assessment of soil strength (Section 16.3.1) in the B horizon under moist conditions. May need assessment of failure mode (Section 16.4) over a range of moisture conditions to rule out oxidic or cutanoxidic horizons; and may need assessment of sensitivity (Section 16.7) and stickiness (Section 16.9) to rule out allophanic soil materials.
Podzol Soils: may need unconfined strength (Section 16.3.1) and failure mode (Section 16.4) tests to help identify a Podzolic B horizon, as well as the presence of humus- and ortstein-pans.
Allophanic Soils: may need assessment of sensitivity (Section 16.7) and stickiness (Section 16.9) to help confirm the presence of allophanic soil materials.
Melanic Soils: may require stickiness assessment (Section 16.9) in the B horizon.
Semiarid Soils: may require cementation tests (Section 16.12) to confirm fragipan absence.
Oxidic Soils: may need assessment of ped strength (Section 16.3.2), soil strength (Section 16.3.1), and failure mode (Section 16.4) over a range of moisture conditions to confirm presence of an oxidic horizon. Stickiness (Section 16.9) and plasticity (Section 16.8) may also be helpful.
Granular Soils: may need assessment of ped strength (Section 16.3.2), soil strength (Section 16.3.1), and failure mode (Section 16.4) over a range of moisture conditions to confirm presence of a cutanoxidic horizon. Stickiness (Section 16.9) and plasticity (Section 16.8) may also be helpful.
Pallic Soils: may require a negative cementation test (Section 16.12) to help identify any fragipans. May require assessment of failure mode (Section 16.4) to help confirm a Brittle-B horizon presence. May require ped strength assessment in the B horizon.
Recent Soils: must not have any moderately or very fluid (Section 16.11) layers within 30 cm of the soil surface.

Note: Strength, fluidity, stickiness, mode of failure, and rubbed fibre content tests are also common diagnostic features at the group and subgroup level in the New Zealand Soil Classification.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.2 Cohesion
The nature of the soil materials in each horizon determines what tests can and should be done. The first step is to determine if the sample is cohesive. Cohesion refers to the tendency of soil particles (i.e. grains of sand, silt, and clay) to stick together under pressure due to internal forces of attraction between them. Whether soil materials are cohesive affects which consistence tests can and should be undertaken in each horizon.

Cohesive soil materials adhere together strongly enough so that they do not easily break up into individual grains. They may have plasticity and stickiness characteristics and have a strength that can be measured in unconfined compression. All listed properties, except particle packing, can be described for non-stony, cohesive soils.
Non-cohesive soil materials have no shear resistance other than that developed by internal friction between grains, and will fall apart when disturbed. Non-cohesive soil materials, by definition, have no unconfined dry strength or plasticity, and the only property that can be meaningfully described is degree of packing or particle packing.

The range of properties that can be described in stony, cohesive soils varies with rock fragment content. In practice this depends on the feasibility of obtaining samples for the required tests.
The distinction between cohesive and non-cohesive is recognised by performing remoulding (Section 16.3.3), plasticity (Section 16.8), and dilatancy (Section 16.10) tests in the following sequence (Figure 16.1). Where doubt still remains after these tests have been completed, the dry coherence test (Section 16.2.1) may be necessary.










Figure 16.1: Determining sample cohesion






16.2.1 Dry coherence
This test can be used as the final arbiter for distinguishing cohesive from non-cohesive soils if other test results are inconclusive (e.g. in fine silt).
Procedure

Remould a 30 mm test sample into a cube and air-dry it.
If the cube collapses under its own weight or after being lightly touched, treat the soil as non-cohesive.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.3 Strength
Strength is also known as ‘resistance to crushing’. This property is assessed using hand or body-weight strength, so users must calibrate themselves against the classes in Table 16.2. Drohan et al. (2020) discuss various options for calibration, including the use of pinch gauges or push-pull gauges to learn what different levels of force feel like.
Each of the tests in this section is evaluated against Table 16.2.




Table 16.2: Strength (resistance to crushing) classes















Code
Name
Failure condition
Force required (N)




1
Very Weak
Very gentle force between straight thumb and forefinger
<8


2
Weak
Gentle force between straight thumb and forefinger
8–20


3
Slightly firm
Moderate force between straight thumb and forefinger
20–40


4
Firm
Strong/maximum force between straight thumb and forefinger
40–75


5
Very firm
Cannot crush between locked hands of an average person. Can crush with gentle force underfoot
75–150


6
Hard
Full body weight (~80 kg) applied slowly
150–800


7
Very hard
Withstands full body weight
>800











16.3.1 Unconfined soil strength
Unconfined soil strength describes how strongly soil material resists crushing when not supported by surrounding material. It provides a simple field indicator of structural integrity in cohesive soils. Note the following.

Test at observed field moisture condition.
If a test cube cannot be formed, the result is strength class 1 ‘Very Weak’ (see Table 16.2). This can happen when soil pedality is weak or absent, but also when pedality is strong and peds are small.
This test cannot be reliably performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Perform the test on a minimally disturbed 30 mm cube.
Hold the cube between thumb and forefinger. Both digits must be straight and fully extended.
Pinch down. If the cube can be crushed, rate the difficulty using categories 1–4 in Table 16.2.
If the cube cannot be crushed by hand, attempt to crush it slowly underfoot, against a hard surface. Rate the difficulty using categories 5–7 in Table 16.2.



16.3.2 Unconfined aggregate strength
Unconfined aggregate strength describes the physical integrity of soil aggregates (peds) under natural conditions. It provides a simple field indicator of soil structural stability in response to management practices and different environmental conditions, but note the following.

Test at observed field moisture condition.
Only peds 30 mm or larger can be reliably tested, but peds larger than 50 mm should be trimmed down to 30 mm.
This test cannot be reliably performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Perform the test on an extracted ped.
Hold the ped between thumb and forefinger. Both digits must be straight and fully extended.
Pinch down. If the ped can be crushed, rate the difficulty using categories 1–4 in Table 16.2.
If the ped cannot be crushed by hand, attempt to crush it slowly underfoot, against a hard surface. Rate the difficulty using categories 5–7 in Table 16.2.



16.3.3 Remoulded soil strength
This test determines the strength of the soil after significant disturbance and reworking, disrupting the structure and any other binding materials like plant roots. Note the following.

Test at observed field moisture condition.
Perform the test on an extracted 30 mm cube or sample of equivalent volume.
This test may be performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Perform the test on an extracted 30 mm cube or sample of equivalent volume.
Place the sample in a small plastic bag and seal with the air excluded (this maintains field moisture content while remoulding). Work the sample until its structure is completely broken down. This may take several minutes.
Still in the bag, remould the soil into a cube and assess its strength against Table 16.2.
Use Table 16.6 to also record the ratio of unconfined to remoulded strength (‘sensitivity’, Section 16.7).

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.4 Mode of failure
Failure is the manner in which unconfined soil yields to increasing stress. This property varies with soil moisture content. Note the following.

Test at observed field moisture condition.
Perform the test on a minimally disturbed 30 mm cube, or an aggregate.
If diagnosing oxidic or cutanoxidic soil material for the New Zealand Soil Classification, repeat the test under dry to wet moisture conditions.

Procedure

Perform the unconfined strength test according to Section 16.3.1.
At strengths of class 5 or less mode of failure can be observed. Assess and record according to Table 16.3.





Table 16.3: Failure mode classes














Code
Name
Description




N
Not determinable
Soil is either too dry or too wet to reliably test.


V
Very friable
Test specimen cannot be formed, or crumbles under very slight stress on crushing within the hand, into aggregates predominantly <2 mm in size. In most instances the test specimen is difficult to obtain.


F
Friable
Test sample cannot be formed, or crumbles under very slight stress on crushing within the hand, into aggregates predominantly >2 mm in size, or crumbles under slight stress on crushing within the hand into aggregates predominantly <2 mm in size.


B
Brittle
Under slowly increasing pressure between extended thumb and forefinger a test specimen retains its size and shape with few or no cracks until it fractures abruptly into aggregates predominantly >2 mm in size.


S
Semi-deformable
Under increasing pressure between extended thumb and forefinger the test specimen as a whole is perceptibly compressed in the direction along which pressure is exerted, but cracks develop and the specimen ruptures before it has been compressed to half its original thickness. Before rupture, parts crumble and fall away if the specimen is shaken while held between thumb and forefinger.


D
Deformable
Under slowly increasing pressure between extended thumb and forefinger, the test specimen can be compressed to at least half its original thickness without the appearance of cracks and without rupture.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.5 Particle packing
Particle packing assesses the stability of a non-cohesive soil. Note the following.

Test only on soils where unconfined strength (Section 16.3.1) cannot be assessed (e.g. gravelly, cobbly or bouldery soils, or loose sands)
This test requires a large pit or exposure.
Do not test at wet or saturated field moisture conditions, as this is unsafe.

Procedure

Expose the soil profile.
Assess ease of excavating and maintaining a vertical face using Table 16.4.





Table 16.4: Particle-packing classes for non-cohesive soils














Code
Name
Description




1
Loose
Easily dislodged by spade or pick; does not maintain a vertical face


2
Compact
Intermediate between loose and dense


3
Dense
Difficult to dislodge except with spade and by removing individual fragments; maintains a stable vertical face


4
Very dense
Very difficult to dislodge except by pick and removing individual fragments; maintains a stable vertical face
















Note 16.2: Use of the Singleton blade





The Singleton blade was a device invented in the 1980s by the New Zealand pedologist Peter Singleton to improve the packing density assessment methods available at the time. The device was a thin, flexible piece of metal with a notched blade, which was inserted into the pit face, leaving a longer end protruding. A pocket penetrometer was then used to push the protruding end of the blade sideways until it reached 45° or the blade fell out of the pit face. The penetrometer reading was empirically correlated to packing density. Mention of this device can be found in many New Zealand soil publications from ~1980 to -2000 (Griffiths et al. 1999), but was not made commercially available and is now rarely used.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.6 Penetration resistance
Penetration resistance is the capacity of the soil, in its natural confined state, to resist penetration by rigid objects. This property is commonly related to strength by empirical means (Table 16.5). Note the following.

This test requires a large pit or exposure.

Procedure

Expose a soil profile.
Assess ease of penetrating a vertical face using Table 16.5.







Note 16.3: Use of pocket penetrometers





Pocket-sized penetrometers with a 6 mm flat tip are often recommended for assessing penetration resistance of cohesive materials in the field. These devices can usually measure no more than 400–1,000 kPa and so may not be adequate for measurements of hard materials.
If a pocket penetrometer is used, take at least 10 readings from across the target horizon and record a median and range for resistance. The soil material being measured must be at or near field capacity when measured for the readings to be valid.







Table 16.5: Penetration resistance classes















Code
Name
Description
Pressure (kPa)




1

Easily penetrated by fist
0–500


2
Very low
Easily penetrated by thumb
500–1,000


3
Low
Readily indented by thumb but penetrated with considerable effort. Imprinted by finger with some effort
1,000–1,500


4
Moderate
Readily indented by thumbnail
1,500–2,200


5
High
Barely imprinted by thumb or forefinger
2,200–3,000


6
Very high
Indented by thumbnail. No imprint by thumb or finger
3,000–4,000


7

Barely indented by thumbnail
>4,000

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.7 Sensitivity
The sensitivity of a soil reflects the extent to which its structure contributes to its strength, and how that strength is reduced when the structure is destroyed. In soils with an unconfined strength class of 4 firm or greater, sensitivity is reported as the ratio of unconfined soil strength (Section 16.3.1) to remoulded strength (Section 16.3.3). For soils with an unconfined strength class of 1–3, the ‘shear test’ is performed. The two methods are assigned equivalent classes in Table 16.6. Note the following.

Test soil in a moist or wet state.
Perform the test on a minimally disturbed 30 mm sample cube.
This test cannot be reliably performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Hold the sample cube between extended thumb and forefinger, as for Section 16.3.
Pinch and press the sample to create a lateral ‘shear’ force, moving the finger forward and down over the thumb.
Assess the sample behaviour against Table 16.6.







Warning 16.1: Other similar tests





This test is not analogous to the shear vane-based sensitivity test of Burns et al. (2005) and cannot be used as a substitute.







Table 16.6: Sensitivity (strength loss on remoulding) classes















Code
Name
Relative strength loss on remoulding (classes)
Shear test behaviour




1
Non-sensitive
0–1
The sample does not smear under shear force and may soften only slightly.


2
Weakly sensitive
2
The sample smears and skids under moderate shear force (20–40 kPa).


3
Moderately sensitive
3
The sample suddenly turns fluid under moderate shear force (20–40 kPa) and the fingers skid. Some free water is evident on fingers after shearing.


4
Very sensitive
>3
The soil suddenly turns fluid and slippery under only gentle shear force (<20 kPa). Free water is easily seen on the fingers after shearing.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.8 Plasticity
Plasticity is the capacity of soil material to change shape continuously when stress is applied and to retain that shape after the removal of stress. Plasticity can help distinguish clayey from silty textures, with silts having relatively low plasticity. Note the following.

Test soil in a wet state.
Perform the test on 3-4 cm3 of soil (a 15–20 mm cube).
This test may be performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Thoroughly remould the sample, keeping it in a wet state.
Adjust the water content to slightly above the plastic limit. In practice this water content is slightly above that at which a 4 mm diameter roll of sample crumbles, but less than that when a sample becomes sticky (Section 16.9), if stickiness is exhibited.
Attempt to roll the sample out into a rod 40 mm long. Assess the minimum achievable diameter of the rod and its behaviour using Table 16.7. To test whether the roll will support its own weight, attempt to pick it up from one end and see if the roll breaks.





Table 16.7: Plasticity classes














Code
Name
Description




1
Non-plastic
A roll 40 mm long and 6 mm thick that supports its own weight cannot be formed.


2
Slightly plastic
A roll 40 mm long and 6 mm thick can be formed and will support its own weight, but a roll 4 mm thick will not support its own weight.


3
Moderately plastic
A roll 40 mm long and 4 mm diameter can be formed, and will support its own weight, but a roll 2 mm thick will not support its own weight.


4
Very plastic
A roll 40 mm long and 2 mm thick can be formed and will support its own weight.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.9 Stickiness
Stickiness is the degree to which remoulded soil adheres to external objects. Stickiness can suggest the presence of clay (particularly 2:1 phyllosilicates) and has agricultural and mechanical implications (e.g. root crop harvesting can be difficult in sticky materials, as can excavation).

Test soil in a wet state.
Perform the test on 3–4 cm3 of soil (a 15–20 mm cube).
This test may be performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Thoroughly remould the sample, keeping it in a wet state.
Press the remoulded material between thumb and forefinger and note its adherence to the fingers.
Adjust the water content by working the sample in the hand to remove water, or by adding water as necessary to achieve the maximum stickiness that the material will exhibit.
Assess maximum stickiness and record using Table 16.8.





Table 16.8: Stickiness classes














Code
Name
Description




1
Non-sticky
After release of pressure, practically no soil material adheres to the thumb or forefinger.


2
Slightly sticky
After release of pressure, soil material adheres perceptibly to both thumb and forefinger but, as the digits are separated it tends to come off one or the other cleanly. The material is not stretched appreciably when the thumb and finger are separated.


3
Moderately sticky
After release of pressure, soil material adheres to both thumb and forefinger and tends to stretch somewhat and pull apart rather than pulling free from either digit.


4
Very sticky
After release of pressure, soil material adheres so strongly to both thumb and forefinger that it is decidedly stretched when they are separated and finally pulls apart leaving part of the soil on the thumb and part on the forefinger.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.10 Dilatancy
Dilatancy occurs due to volume change during shearing and is used as a criterion for distinguishing non-cohesive from cohesive soil materials. The test can also help to determine the relative dominance of silt and clay (silty textures are more prone to exhibiting dilatant behaviour). Note the following.

Test soil in a moist to wet state.
Perform the test on 3-4 cm3 of soil (a 15–20 mm cube).
This test may be performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Adjust the soil to a moist to wet state.
Roll into a ball ~30 mm in diameter.
Hold the sample in an upturned palm and slap the back of the hand containing the sample several times with the other hand, or shake the hand vigorously from side to side.

A dilatant reaction is shown by a shiny surface caused by water extrusion, and by a dull surface when the palm of the hand is folded to partly remould the sample, causing water to be drawn into the sample. Dilatant samples will also lose their ball shape, flattening down. Record dilatant behaviour as a binary: true/false.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.11 Fluidity
Fluidity tests whether saturated soils have an unconfined strength that is largely eliminated by saturation. Such materials were generally emplaced under water, have never been drained, have a fine texture that minimises gravity-based settling, and are not overlain by enough other sediment to have been compressed. Note the following.

Test soil at a saturated state.
Only test soils that are saturated under field conditions.
Perform the test on ~200 cm3 of soil (a large handful).
This test may be performed on auger-extracted samples.

Procedure

Extract the sample and squeeze firmly in the hand.
Evaluate the sample’s behaviour using Table 16.9.





Table 16.9: Fluidity classes














Code
Name
Description




1
Slightly fluid
Some material tends to flow into the spaces between the fingers, but after full pressure is exerted most of the residue is left in the hand.


2
Moderately fluid
Soil material flows easily between the fingers, but a small residue is left in the hand after full pressure is exerted.


3
Very fluid
Soil material flows like a slightly viscous liquid between the fingers, and very little or no residue is left in the hand after full pressure is exerted.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.12 Induration
Induration is the degree to which soil particles are held together by some combination of cementation and close packing. Note the following.

Perform the test on a minimally disturbed 30 mm cube or aggregate.
This test may also be performed on individual nodules and other solids <30 mm.
This test cannot be reliably performed on auger-extracted samples.
This test requires a minimum 1 hour to complete and can be done immediately following fieldwork.

Equipment
This test requires:

a sponge (~50 mm diameter, flat)
deionised water
a sample container at least 40–50 mm deep.

Procedure

Test the soil strength at field-moist condition, according to Section 16.3.1.
Place the sample on a wet sponge until thoroughly moistened, then immerse the sample in deionised water for 1 hour.
If the sample has not slaked (see Section 17.8), retest the soil strength of the wet sample according to Section 16.3.1.
Assess the behaviour of the sample using Table 16.10.





Table 16.10: Induration classes














Code
Name
Description




1
Non-indurated
Sample slakes within 1 hour


2
Very weakly indurated
Has not slaked; strength class of 2–4


3
Weakly indurated
Strength class of 5–6


4
Strongly indurated
Strength class of 7, but will break when struck by a sharp blow with a hammer


5
Very strongly indurated
Strength class of 7, and does not break when struck by a sharp blow with a hammer.

title: 16  Consistence
text:
16.13 Rubbed fibre content
Rubbed fibre content is an indicator of the degree of organic decomposition and can be used to help determine whether organic material qualifies as fibric, mesic or humic (Section 14.1.3.1, Section 18.2.2). Note the following.

This test can be performed on any sample with an appreciable amount of visible and decomposing organic matter. Live plant roots should be removed before performing the test.
This test can be performed on auger-extracted samples. However, exercise caution when extracting samples from below the water-table as they may easily become cross-contaminated by overlying material.
Perform the test on ~100 cm3 of soil (a small handful).
Perform the test on wet materials.

Procedure

Extract the sample and squeeze to remove excess water
Rub the wet sample 10 times between the thumb and forefinger, or knead a ball of sample 10 times firmly in the palm of the hand.
Examine the proportion of visible plant fibres.

Note that larger pieces of rotting solid or soft timber (e.g. buried branches) should be included in the total proportion of fibrous material.




Table 16.11: Fibric organic material classes














Code
Name
Description




1
None
No appreciable fibre


2
Minor
Fibrous material <15%


3
Moderate
Fibrous material 15–75%


4
Major
Fibrous material >75%

Wellington, New Zealand, New Zealand Geotechnical Society. https://www.nzgs.org/libraries/field-description-of-soil-and-rock/


Drohan PJ, Thompson JA, Lindbo DL, Beaudette DE, Dadio SD 2020. Redefining the fragipan to improve field recognition and land use relevance. Soil Science Society of America Journal 84(4): 1055–1066. https://doi.org/10.1002/saj2.20098

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.1 Field pH
Field tests, which involve application of chemical reagents to small test specimens of fresh soil, support confident soil profile descriptions in the field by providing immediate indications of key soil chemical properties. As well as informing the description itself, the tests can help guide sampling decisions and the later choice of laboratory analyses. In some cases they can act as quality control measures (e.g. large inconsistencies in pH between field and laboratory may indicate unwanted sample oxidation in acid sulfate soils).
Field tests do have limited precision and accuracy compared to their laboratory equivalents due to their simplicity and short observation times. Where field tests are not conclusive, laboratory testing may still be warranted.
Field tests should be performed down-profile, with at least one sample tested per horizon. Samples should be taken from the mid-point of each horizon, and extracted with clean hands or tools to avoid cross-contamination. Additional samples in transition zones may also be of interest. Properties within the upper part of the first B horizon can be diagnostic in soil classification.
Soil pH is a critical indicator of soil composition and behaviour, as well as its suitability for specific uses (Mosley et al. 2024). Soil pH can also help indicate a potential environmental hazard, or a pollution event.
Soil pH varies at multiple scales: across the landscape in response to changes in parent material, vegetation and climate, down the soil profile, and even at short range within soil horizons. Field measurements of soil pH can provide information on down-profile variability and help contextualise the profile within its surrounds.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.1.1 Colorimetric field pH (pHf)
This method, following Raupach and Tucker (1959), requires the use of a pre-made kit containing universal pH indicator, barium sulfate powder, and a calibrated colour card for interpreting the results. These kits can be purchased at hardware or garden supply stores, as well as at specialist environmental field supply stores. The tests are simple but only precise to ± 0.5 units, and accurate (vs laboratory-based testing) to around the same degree. They are usually valid over a pH range of 2–10.
Equipment
This test requires a field pH kit, which contains:

universal indicator
barium sulfate powder
calibrated colour interpretation card
small sample containers or plastic tray
stirring stick.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into a small container. Mix or crush the sample lightly to break open small peds.
Sprinkle the sample surface with just enough barium sulfate powder to cover it. This is used to make it easier to see the pH indicator colour.
Add a couple of drops of pH indicator. Match the indicator colour to the card provided and record the pH of the closest match (e.g. 40 cm: 5.5). Do not interpolate between chips. Do not wait to read the pH: readings are unreliable after the sample has dried.







Note 17.2: Sources of variation between field pH and laboratory pH





Some variability between colorimetric field pH and laboratory pH is expected. Reasons for the variability may include the following.

The quality of the reagents in use, the kit’s age, and how carefully it has been stored may all vary. The dye recipe needs to have been followed accurately so that the resulting colours match the calibration card. Impurities in the supplied barium sulfate powder can also cause issues. The calibration card itself needs to be printed with accurate colours, waterproofed, and not left to bleach in the sun.
Operators need full colour vision to interpret the card correctly. While diagnosed colour blindness is relatively rare, many people have minor colour-recognition limitations without knowing it. Taking a colour vision test periodically is recommended.
Samples taken for laboratory analysis may change pH during transport, while in storage, or during sample processing.






17.1.2 Field pH in water (pHfw)
Measure pHfw with a field-ready electronic pH meter. Electronic meters are precise and can usually measure the full 0–14 pH range, but they are sensitive to temperature fluctuations and must be regularly calibrated. Always refer to the device manual for specific maintenance requirements.
Equipment
This test requires:

a field-ready electronic pH meter (ideally with a temperature sensor)
deionised or demineralised water
small sample containers (e.g. 50 mL centrifuge tubes)
stirring sticks.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into a small container. Mix with deionised or demineralised water to a loose paste, ensuring the mix is deep enough for the pH probe tip to be adequately covered.
Insert the pH probe into the sample and wait for the reading to stabilise to 1 decimal place. Stability is indicated by no change for 10 seconds. Do not stir the sample with the probe.
Record the reading and the depth it was taken from (e.g. 40 cm: 5.2).
Thoroughly rinse the probe before testing the next sample.







Tip 17.1: Sample handling



Make sure to sample with clean hands: tests can easily be contaminated by residues. In particular, sunscreens will cause a falsely high pH reading.




17.1.3 Field pH in hydrogen peroxide (pHfox)
Field pH in concentrated hydrogen peroxide (30% H2O2) is paired with field pH in water to diagnose the presence of FeS2 (iron sulfide, or pyrite) and thus the presence of sulfidic soil materials. A significant drop in pHfox vs pHfw is considered diagnostic; see the discussion in Sullivan et al. (2018a), section A1.4.4 for further details.
The following method is reproduced from Sullivan et al. (2018a), section A1.4.3.
Equipment
This test requires:

field-ready electronic pH meter (ideally with a temperature sensor)
concentrated hydrogen peroxide (30% H2O2)
deionised or demineralised water
small sample containers (e.g. 50 mL centrifuge tubes) without lids
stirring sticks.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into each tube.
Add enough H2O2 to cover each sample, and stir briefly. Do not cap and shake the tubes.
Allow up to 15 minutes for any reaction to occur, especially in cool weather. Placing the rack in the sun may help progress the reaction. Note that strong reactions can sometimes occur almost instantly. Observe the samples from a short distance (>0.5 m) and do not peer into the tubes.
Where reactions occur, record their violence using the scale in Table 17.1. If excessive, the reaction may be tamped down by adding a very small amount of deionised water.
Where reactions occur, wait for them to settle and add a little more H2O2. Repeat until the reaction no longer occurs.
Once reactions have fully completed and the tubes have cooled, measure the pH of each sample with the electronic meter. Record to the nearest 0.1 units as for pHfw, and rinse the probe thoroughly between readings.







Warning 17.2: Safe handling and preparation of hydrogen peroxide






Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is highly corrosive. Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling, and in a field situation make sure that there is access to plenty of clean water for rinsing.
Before bringing H2O2 into the field it must be buffered to pH 4.5–5.5. While stirring, add a few drops of dilute NaOH and regularly check the pH with a calibrated electrode until the correct range is reached. Allow the H2O2 to stand for 15 minutes and then recheck the pH.
H2O2 degrades over time, so only buffer small quantities at a time and refrigerate when not in use.
In the field, H2O2 containers should be kept out of direct sunlight and preferably in a small cooler, because excessive heat will cause the H2O2 to break down, releasing oxygen. This can cause its container to rupture or spray its contents when opened. Only take small containers into the field, and monitor them for signs of elevated internal pressure (e.g. bulging). Make sure all containers are clearly labelled.








Table 17.1: Hydrogen peroxide reaction strength ratings














Code
Name
Description




N
No reaction
No fizzing or bubbling after 15 minutes


L
Slight reaction
Sample fizzes or bubbles slightly but does not steam


M
Moderate reaction
Sample bubbles and steams slightly but does not completely boil; unlikely to continue reacting if more peroxide is added.


H
High reaction
Sample boils and steams but does not boil over; may continue to react when more peroxide is added.


X
Explosive reaction
Sample rapidly boils over and gives off considerable steam; likely to continue to react when more peroxide is added.
















Note 17.3: Incubation methods for acid sulfate soils





Field-adjacent incubation methods are available as an alternative low-cost method of identifying acid sulfate soils. These involve minimal equipment and no hazardous chemicals, but can take up to 3 months to complete. See Sullivan et al. (2018b), Appendix C, for further information.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.2 Electrical conductivity (ECf)
The soil solution’s ECf is an estimate of its soluble salt content, which can affect plant nutrition and water uptake. Salinity is a diagnostic criterion in the New Zealand Soil Classification, used in the Gley, Semiarid, Recent and Raw Soil Orders. In New Zealand a 1:5 ratio of soil to water is used in the laboratory, so this must be matched in the field.
Equipment
This test requires:

a field-ready electrical conductivity meter (ideally with a temperature sensor)
deionised or demineralised water
small sample containers (e.g. 50 mL centrifuge tubes) with lids.
stirring sticks.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, place soil in each tube up to the 5 mL mark. Top up with water to 30 mL.
Cap and shake each sample vigorously for 30 seconds, then allow the samples to settle for a few minutes.
Use the EC meter to record the solution conductivity. Report to the nearest 0.1 dS/m.
Rinse the probe thoroughly between measurements.







Note 17.4: Conductivity units





EC is most commonly reported in units of millisiemens per centimetre (mS/cm) or decisiemens per metre (dS/m), which are numerically equivalent. Other units less commonly used require specific conversion (e.g. electronic meters may report in µS/cm, where 1 mS/cm = 1,000 µS/cm.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.3 Calcium carbonate (Caf)
While large chunks of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) in the form of shells or calcareous rocks are easy to spot, CaCO3 in the fine earth is not, and there can also be some doubt about the composition of secondary features. This test should be considered when working in areas where calcareous rocks occur near the land surface, where field pH is >7, or when white or pale concentrations or coatings are observed, such as in some Pallic Soils and Semiarid Soils.
CaCO3 reacts with acidic solutions in a neutralisation reaction, releasing water, carbon dioxide, and heat as the carbonate becomes a salt (calcium chloride, CaCl2). The reaction is rapid and causes a soil sample to ‘fizz’ visibly. 10% (or 1 M) HCl is used for this test because it is stable, cheap, and relatively safe, while still reacting vigorously.
Note that dolomitic carbonates (CaMg(CO3)2) may not react noticeably to this strength of acid in the field, and may require laboratory identification.
Equipment

10% or 1 M HCl, stored in a small dropper bottle
small sample containers or a plastic tray.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into a small container. Lightly crush to break up peds and/or concentrations.
Using a dropper bottle, add a drop or two of HCl and observe closely.
Record the vigour of the reaction using Table 17.2.

HCl can also be applied directly to a soil profile exposure, but be careful not to include the tested patches in any other soil samples.






Warning 17.3: Safe handling and preparation of HCl






HCl is corrosive. Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling, and in a field situation make sure there is access to plenty of clean water for rinsing.
Do not transport large quantities of HCl, even if dilute. A 25–50 mL bottle will normally last for weeks of fieldwork.
Make sure HCl containers are clearly labelled and corrosion-resistant.








Table 17.2: Hydrochloric acid reaction ratings














Code
Name
Description




N
No reaction
No audible or visible fizzing


L
Slight reaction
Fizzing faintly audible and barely visible


M
Moderate reaction
Fizzing audible and clearly visible; small bubbles of ≤3 mm diameter


H
High reaction
Fizzing easily audible and visible, bubbles up to 7 mm diameter
















Note 17.5: Measuring CaCO3





While Milne et al. (1995) and some other publications (Kalra and Maynard 1991; Rayment and Lyons 2011) have attempted to use the degree of fizzing to estimate CaCO3 percentage content, the estimates and descriptions of fizzing vary and are not considered highly reliable. If a precise numeric estimate of CaCO3 percentage is required, it should be measured under laboratory conditions.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.4 Manganese (Mnf)
Manganese-rich concentrations in soil are dark to black (sometimes bluish-black; e.g. pyrolusite (Churchman and Lowe 2012)) and often very small, so they may be missed or mistaken for other minerals. Manganese oxides react to H2O2 in a similar fashion to iron sulfide (see Section 17.1.3). This test uses a safer, dilute H2O2 solution. The test should be considered where dark flecks are observed in the soil profile, particularly under imperfect to poor drainage conditions (see Section 19.1). Larger manganese oxide concretions will also generate a brown streak on a streak plate or white paper (whereas charcoal, in contrast, will generate a black streak).
Equipment
This test requires:

dilute (3–6%) H2O2 solution, stored in a small dropper bottle
small sample containers or a plastic tray.

Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into a small container. Lightly crush to break up peds and/or concentrations.
Using a dropper bottle, add a drop or two of dilute H2O2 and observe closely for fizzing.
Record the presence or absence of a reaction (e.g. 40 cm: ✔).

Dilute H2O2 can also be applied directly to a soil exposure, but be careful not to include the tested patches in any soil samples. Note that H2O2 will also react with organic material, so this test is not definitive in highly organic samples. Using concentrated H2O2 will increase the likelihood of misinterpretation because it will attack organic material more vigorously.

title: 17  Field tests
section: 17.5 Reactive aluminium by sodium fluoride reaction (NaFf)
text:
17.5 Reactive aluminium by sodium fluoride reaction (NaFf)
This test indicates the presence of reactive hydroxy-aluminium sites on soil minerals. In New Zealand these sites are most often associated with the presence of the nanocrystalline clay mineral allophane, along with imogolite (which has both long-range and short-range order). Reactive hydroxy-aluminium sites can also be found on ferrihydrite and aluminium-humus complexes, especially in podzolic B horizons.
The principle of the method is that fluoride ions at about pH 7 react with hydroxy-aluminium to release hydroxyl ions, causing a rise in pH (Fieldes and Perrott 1966). The test conditions have been chosen so that the released OH– from soils containing reactive hydroxy-aluminium turn phenolphthalein indicator reagent red (pH >9), while most other soils remain at lower pH values so that the indicator remains colourless.
Equipment
This test requires:

saturated aqueous sodium fluoride (NaF) solution (1 M NaF, maintained in the presence of an excess of undissolved NaF)
filter paper (Whatman No. 42 or similar) treated with phenolphthalein indicator (0.5% dissolved in 50% ethanol) and subsequently dried.

The solution and treated paper both degrade over time and should not be stored for more than a few months.
Procedure

With clean hands or a small scoop, place ~0.5 cm3 soil onto a piece of pre-treated filter paper. Lightly crush to break up peds and put the soil in firm contact with the paper.
Using a dropper bottle, add a drop or two of 1 M NaF (enough to wet the sample but not flood it) and wait up to 2 minutes.
Record the reaction intensity using Table 17.3 (e.g. 40 cm: M).







Warning 17.4: Safe handling and preparation of NaF






NaF is toxic and an irritant to skin and eyes. Wear safety glasses and gloves when handling, and in a field situation make sure there is access to plenty of clean water for rinsing.
Make sure NaF containers are clearly labelled.








Table 17.3: Sodium fluoride reaction ratings















Code
Name
Description
Colour




N
No reaction
No colour change



Circle






L
Slight reaction
Paper turns faint pink within two minutes



Circle






M
Moderate reaction
Paper turns moderate pink, usually within 30 seconds



Circle






H
Strong reaction
Paper turns dark pink, usually within 10 seconds



Circle




















Important 17.1: Use caution interpreting the NaFf test






The presence of alkaline conditions and/or free CO32- will cause a strong false positive for this test, as the NaF will precipitate to CaF2 and yield Na2CO3. When in doubt, pre-screen with 10% HCl or a field pH test to avoid confusion.
The presence of organic matter can interfere with the test by buffering the pH change.
Soils containing free aluminium (Al3+) may also react.










Note 17.6: NaFf test interpretation





Reactivity ratings used to interpret the NaFf test have been inconsistently presented over the decades since their original publication, with a tendency to get more complicated over time. The reactivity ratings presented in Table 17.3 are a return to the simpler schemas seen in early reporting.
While a strong correlation can be made between phosphate retention and NaF reaction intensity within younger tephra-derived soils (Allophanic and Pumice Soil orders), the correlation does not hold across all soils.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.6 Reducing conditions
Reducing conditions can be suggested by low-chroma soil colours (see Note 13.2), redox mottling, and other indicators of poor drainage. More confident diagnoses can be made by including field testing for reduced iron (Fe2+) because an indicator of persistently reducing conditions.
Rapid testing for Fe2+ can be accomplished using 2,2’-bipyridine (previously/also known as ⍺-⍺-dipyridyl) dye, which turns pinkish red in the presence of Fe2+ (Childs 1981; Vepraskas 2015). Test strips are also commercially available and may prove easier to use in the field (Berkowitz et al. 2017). Note that these tests should only be conducted on wet or moist soils; soils that are in a slightly moist to dry state will not be experiencing reducing conditions. This test may be useful for distinguishing a reduced horizon from a low-chroma eluvial one (see also Section 18.2.4).
Procedure

With clean hands or a small plastic scoop, remove ~1–2 cm3 soil into a small container or onto a surface with a white background.
Depending on the method:

if using indicator strips, press the strip gently against a freshly exposed sample surface for a few seconds, then remove and check for colour change.
if using 2,2’-bipyridine dye, apply a few drops to a freshly exposed sample surface and watch for a colour change.

Record the presence or absence of a reaction (e.g. 40 cm: ✔).

In both cases work quickly because, if reduced, the sample will oxidise rapidly on excavation.






Warning 17.5: False positives





Recent contact with steel tools, previous application of 10% HCl when testing for carbonates (Section 17.3), or exposure to intense sunlight after the dye has been applied can all cause false positive readings for this test (Vepraskas 2015).









Warning 17.6: Safe handling of 2,2’-bipyridine solution





Some manuals have suggested the use of a spray bottle to apply 2,2’-bipyridine to an exposure or extracted sample. This is not recommended due to the chemical’s toxicity. See National Center for Biotechnology Information (2024) for further details. A squirt bottle that does not emit a mist may be a safer choice.









Note 17.7: Other methods of assessing reduction





Current best practice for research-grade monitoring of redox potential in soils involves the use of Indicator of Reduction In Soils (IRIS) devices (Sapkota et al. 2022), sometimes in concert with electronic sensors. IRIS devices require specialist construction, installation for several weeks, and careful post-processing.

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.7 Water repellence
Water repellence in soils results from hydrophobic organic compounds (e.g. plant leaf waxes) accumulating under a specific range of soil moisture conditions (Dekker et al. 2009; Soil Survey Staff 2024). Repellency is thus locally and seasonally variable, and usually confined to surface layers. Water repellence is most commonly assessed by observing absorption of distilled water and/or ethanol into the soil.
Equipment
This test requires:

Deionised or demineralised water, stored in a small dropper bottle
2 M ethanol, stored in a small dropper bottle
Small sample containers or a plastic tray.

Procedure
This test is only reliable on dry soils.

With clean hands or a small scoop, remove ~2–3 cm3 soil into a small container. Leave the sample intact.
Use a dropper or syringe to place 3–5 well-separated drops of distilled water onto the soil surface from a distance of no more than 5 mm. Measure the median time it takes for the drops to be absorbed.
If the water drops take longer than 10 seconds to disappear, repeat the test with a fresh sample and use ethanol.
Record the repellence rating according to Table 17.4.

Note that water repellence is affected by ambient temperature (National Committee on Soil and Terrain 2024, p. 170).




Table 17.4: Water repellence ratings














Code
Name
Description




N
Not repellent
Water is absorbed within 10 seconds


R
Repellent
Water is not absorbed within 10 seconds. Ethanol is absorbed within 10 seconds


S
Strongly repellent
Ethanol is not absorbed within 10 seconds

title: 17  Field tests
text:
17.8 Rapid slaking and dispersion
Soil aggregates can slake, or disintegrate, when wetted up from a dry state as trapped air rushes out of the pore spaces. Over a longer time period clay swelling may also contribute to aggregate breakdown by slaking. Aggregate resistance to slaking behaviour is modified by organic matter content and clay mineral type. Dispersive behaviour also causes aggregate breakdown in water but is driven by a relative dominance of Na+ ions (and to some extent Mg2+ and K+) on ion exchange sites.
Field testing can reveal soils that are prone to rapid slaking and dispersion. However, soils that are only slightly prone to these behaviours may not be detected in the short assessment time described below. The test also requires dry soil samples, which can be hard to come by under New Zealand field conditions. Running the test over a 2 hour period on air-dried peds after fieldwork will often be more useful. The laboratory equivalent assessment runs over a minimum of 20 hours (Emerson 2002; Standards Australia 2017).
Equipment
This test requires:

deionised or demineralised water
a shallow dish, 3–5 cm deep and 15–30 cm in diameter.

Procedure

Set out a testing dish in a sheltered location and fill with at least 2–3 cm of deionised or demineralised water (enough to completely cover added peds). Allow to settle.
Carefully add one or two dry peds from each pedal soil horizon (or 1–2 cm3 of minimally disturbed material from a massive horizon), working clockwise around the dish. Minimise disturbing the water.
Observe the samples after waiting 10 minutes. Rate their slaking behaviour using Table 17.5. Rate their dispersive behaviour using Table 17.6.





Table 17.5: Slaking behaviour ratings














Code
Name
Description




N
No slaking
Peds remain intact. Some bubbles may develop on their surfaces.


P
Partial slaking
Peds have broken open or partially collapsed, mostly into smaller peds.


C
Complete slaking
Peds have collapsed into a pile of separated grains, and little to no ped structure remains visible.














Table 17.6: Dispersion behaviour ratings














Code
Name
Description




N
No dispersion
Peds remain intact and water remains clear.


S
Slight dispersion
Peds remain largely intact, but a faint milky halo of suspended clay particles can be seen around them.


M
Moderate dispersion
Peds partly collapse and a milky halo is visible around the sample


C
Complete dispersion
Peds have collapsed into a pile of separate grains and are surrounded by an extensive and dense halo.
