title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.1 Primary designations
Pedological horizon notation operates as a shorthand for describing the full profile, making it easier to compare and contrast groups of profiles, and to classify them. Horizons are given a particular designation according to their position in the profile, and according to soil properties that reflect the kind and degree of pedogenic alteration of the parent material.
Becuase designations are made in the field they are defined mainly by morphological properties that differentiate horizons from those above or below, or from a presumed parent material. Laboratory data may be needed to confirm identification, especially in marginal cases.
The current scheme for New Zealand reported here was developed largely from the system used in England and Wales (Avery 1980) by Clayden and Hewitt (2015), and is broadly similar to those used overseas (e.g. the World Reference Base for Soil Resources (IUSS Working Group WRB 2022), Soil Taxonomy (Soil Survey Staff 2022)). However, note that there are significant differences in suffix use between all of these systems as they have become adapted to regional conditions.
Codes for primary horizon designations (previously known as master horizons) can be used by themselves for rapid assessment, or where criteria for more detailed nomenclature are not met. Always capitalised, they are grouped into two organic horizons (L, O) and five mineral horizons (A, E, B, C, R) as per Table 18.1.
Table 18.1: Primary horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




L
Litter
Organic horizon accumulated under dry conditions. It is saturated with water for no more than 30 consecutive days in most years.


O
Peat
Organic horizon accumulated under wet conditions. It is saturated with water for at least 30 consecutive days in most years, or has been artificially drained.


A
Surface
Mineral horizon formed at the surface or below an organic horizon. It is characterised by incorporation of humified organic matter, or properties resulting from disturbance by cultivation. The organic matter has been incorporated by biological activity, shrink–swell behaviour, or mixing through cultivation, rather than by translocation.


E
Eluviated


A subsurface mineral horizon that contains less organic matter and/or iron and/or clay than the horizon immediately below as a result of downward or lateral movement. It is identified by having ALL of the following:


a moist colour value of 4 or more, or a dry colour value of 5 or more, with or without silty or sandy coatings observable in a dry specimen
a higher colour value or lower chroma combined with less well-developed pedality and/or coarser texture than an underlying B horizon
less organic matter and a higher colour value than an overlying H, O or A horizon.

The colour of the horizon can be that of uncoated sand and silt grains, but E horizons are also recognised where coats of iron oxides or other minerals mask the colour of the primary particles.


B
Subsoil


A subsurface mineral horizon having little to no remnant geological structure in residual materials or fine stratification in transported materials, characterised by one or more of the following:


illuvial concentration of silicate clay, iron, manganese, aluminium or organic matter, alone or in some combination
coatings of sesquioxides that give the horizon a lower colour value, a higher chroma, or a redder hue than the horizons above and below, without apparent illuviation of iron
alteration that has formed silicate clay or liberated oxides, or both, and that leads to ped formation
evidence of solution and removal of carbonates.

A B horizon is differentiated from adjacent horizons by moist and dry colour and/or pedality, and normally underlies an A or E horizon.


C
Weathering substrate


An unconsolidated or weakly consolidated mineral horizon that is little affected by pedogenic processes and lacks properties of A, E or B horizons. The material may be either like or unlike that from which the solum presumably formed. A C horizon may have been modified by development of low-chroma colour and/or colour patterns caused by wetting and drying cycles, or accumulation of carbonates or more soluble salts.

Some highly weathered regolithic or saprolithic materials (see weathering) are designated C rather than CR (see transitional horizons) if the material does not meet the requirements of A, E or B horizons.


R
Rock
Hard or very hard bedrock that is impracticable to dig with a spade. The rock may exhibit limited signs of weathering, such as cracks, but these are generally too few and too small for significant root development. However, trees and shrubs do root into fissures in R horizons. R horizons may qualify as paralithic or lithic material.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
Note 18.1: L Horizons





Note that the L horizon was previously used to describe fresh leaf litter, but such materials are now not considered part of the profile description and so this designation has been removed. Fresh litter presence is described as part of surface cover assessment (Section 10.3). The L horizon now unites the former F and H horizons.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.2 Secondary designations
Note that C and R horizons have no secondary designations.

18.2.1 L horizons




Table 18.2: Secondary L horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




Lf
Fibric litter
An L horizon that consists mainly of plant remains that are no longer fresh but remain readily identifiable in terms of botanical origin (e.g. lightly decomposed leaves, fronds, or twigs).


Lm
Mesic litter
An L horizon that consists mainly of partially decomposed organic matter, where fragments of recognisable plant tissues may be identified but whole plant parts are no longer observable


Lh
Humic litter
An L horizon that consists mainly of strongly decomposed organic matter with few or no identifiable plant remains other than resistant woody fragments >20 mm that cannot be reduced to fibres by crushing and shredding between the fingers.












18.2.2 O horizons




Table 18.3: Secondary O horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




Of
Fibric peat
An O horizon that consists mainly of well-preserved plant remains that are readily identifiable in terms of botanical origin, with at least 75% fibre content by volume after rubbing.


Om
Mesic peat
An O horizon that consists mainly of partially decomposed plant remains, intermediate in fibre content between Of and Oh.


Oh
Humic peat
An O horizon that consists mainly of strongly decomposed organic matter with few or no identifiable plant remains other than resistant woody fragments >20 mm that cannot be reduced to fibres by crushing and shredding between the fingers. The fibre content is less than 15% after rubbing. It is distinguished from a mineral soil horizon by its deformable failure and capacity for shrinkage on drying of 30% or more.



Note: Add the p suffix wherever the O horizon is affected by cultivation (e.g. Ohp).













18.2.3 A Horizons




Table 18.4: Secondary A horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




Ah
Natural
An A horizon in which there is no evident disturbance due to cultivation or pastoral land use.


Ap
Agricultural
An A horizon in which incorporation of organic matter has involved mixing due to cultivation or to increased biological activity associated with fertilisation or irrigation. It may contain material from pre-existing E, B or C horizons.


App
Recently tilled
An Ap horizon consisting mainly of clods and fragments with little pedal material, caused by cultivation during the past year.












18.2.4 E horizons




Table 18.5: Secondary E horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




Ea
Leached


An E horizon in which:


weathered films on sand and silt particles are absent, very thin or discontinuous, so that the colour of the horizon is mainly determined by the colours of uncoated grains, and
redox segregations are absent (see redox suffixes).

It is not saturated with water for prolonged periods and usually overlies a Bh or Bs horizon.


Ed
Densipan


An E horizon that is non-cemented but has high soil strength and bulk density. It meets all of the following requirements:


either
a. unconfined strength is hard or very hard (strength class 6+) at soil moisture states from moist to dry, or
b. soil penetration resistance exceeds 4,000 kPa (penetration resistance class 7+) at soil moisture states from moist to dry, and
moist and dry samples slake in water within 10 minutes.

Densipans occur in soils with felsic parent materials. The strength is due to a close-fit arrangement of sand and silt-sized quartz particles.


Ew
Weathered


An E horizon with a dominantly brownish colour. It has both of the following:


a moist chroma of 4 or more but less than 6, and
<2% redox segregations.

Silt coats, or ‘skeletans’, may be present, and the horizon normally overlies a Bt horizon containing significantly more clay. Where the lower boundary is a lithological discontinuity and there is no clear evidence of an illuvial relationship with the underlying 2B horizon, the notation EBw is used (see transitional horizons)












18.2.5 B Horizons




Table 18.6: Secondary B horizon designations














Code
Name
Description




Bfm
Placic
A sharply defined, cemented, pan-like B horizon usually less than 10 mm thick, but the same designation may be given to horizons up to 25 mm thick. It is black to reddish brown or dark red in colour, and a black upper part can often be distinguished from a reddish brown lower part. It lies roughly parallel to the soil surface but is commonly wavy or convolute. A Bfm horizon usually occurs as a single pan, but in places it can split into two or more layers. It forms a barrier to most roots and restricts water movement.


Bh
Humose


A dark-coloured B horizon of podzolised soils enriched in organic matter, associated with aluminium, or iron and aluminium, as a result of illuviation.

It has a moist value and chroma of 3 or less, or a value of 4 if chroma is 2, dominant in the matrix, and contains 1% or more organic carbon. The fabric has sand- or silt-sized pellet-like aggregates, coats on mineral grains, or both. In some horizons (including humus-pans, Bhm), these coatings have coalesced to fill pores and cement the horizon.


Bo
Oxidic


A strongly weathered B horizon formed in mixed crystalline iron and aluminium oxides and kaolin subgroup minerals, with low-activity clay properties. It must meet all the following requirements.


It has weak or very weak primary ped and soil strength, as determined by the unconfined strength test over moist to dry soil water states.
Unconfined failure is friable or very friable over very moist to dry soil water states. Materials fail to predominantly 3 mm or smaller peds comprising silt- and sand-sized polyhedra and granules.
Primary peds slake in water to stable microaggregates (3 mm or smaller), which show no dispersion or only slight dispersion.
It is non-reactive or very weakly reactive to the reactive aluminium test.
Materials are at most slightly sticky and slightly plastic.

Bo horizons are clayey, with measured clay content commonly exceeding 60%. Measured clay percentage is usually larger than in overlying A horizons, but clay increase is not a defining criterion because of the problem of quantifying clay content in materials that are frequently difficult to disperse.
Clay coatings are either visually absent or only present at frequencies of about 1%. The Bo horizon has low-activity clay accessory properties with ECEC and CEC less than 12 and 16 cmolc/kg clay, respectively.


Bs
Sesquioxides


An ochreous B horizon of podzolised soils containing illuvial aluminium, iron, or both, that is closely associated, or complexed, with illuvial organic matter. The aluminium and iron are apparently mainly present as minerals with short-range order (especially allophane and ferrihydrite), though some aluminium is often present as aluminium-humus.

The designation Bs should be used for B horizons that:

occur below an Ea, Bh, Bfm or a strongly acid A horizon, and
have both a moist value and chroma of more than 3, and
have a rapid positive reaction to the sodium fluoride test.

It is not possible to define the morphology of a Bs horizon such that it can be distinguished from certain Bw horizons enriched in iron and aluminium due to weathering in situ.
Characteristic features of Bs horizons are:

reddest hue and highest chroma at the top of the horizon
earthy apedal fabric with fine spheroids, or weakly developed blocks or polyhedrons
very weak or moderately weak soil strength when moist or dry
a greasy or smeary feel when very moist
low plasticity in relation to clay content
sand- or silt-sized pellet-like aggregates, sesquioxidic coats on mineral grains, or both.

In some horizons (including ortstein-pans, Bsm) coatings have coalesced to fill pores and cement the horizon.


Bt
Argillic


An argillic horizon is a clay-enriched horizon. It has one of the following.


Clay coatings occur that have a waxy lustre when dry and sufficient thickness to envelop fine sand grains.; coatings occur either on peds (10% or more of the ped surfaces), or in pores (in more than one-third of the observed tubular pores), or as bridges between sand grains (in more than half of the horizon); or
the horizon includes at least 15% by cross-sectional area of clay-enriched lamellae (clay bands); or
it contains sufficiently more clay than the overlying horizon, as detected by hand texturing (5% or more), excluding any differences that result from a lithological discontinuity; and either
a. it is overlain by an eluvial (E) horizon and the upper boundary of texture contrast is abrupt or sharp, or
b. clay coatings occur on ped or pore surfaces.




Bw
Weathered


A B horizon that shows evidence of alteration under well-aerated conditions and does not qualify as Bh, Bs or Bt.

To qualify as a Bw rather than BC or C it must meet at least one of the following requirements:

a redder hue or higher chroma than an underlying horizon in similar materials (‘colour B’)
it has spheroids, blocks, polyhedrons, tablets, prisms, columns or plates which distinguish the horizon from a BC or C horizon below (‘structural B’)
there is evidence of either partial or complete decalcification (i.e. less CaCO3 than the underlying horizon, which may contain redeposited carbonates).

A Bw horizon has less than 2% redox segregations (see redox suffixes. It is otherwise distinguished by the following colour requirements:

with moist values less than 5, chromas must be 3 or more.
with moist values 5 or more, chromas must be 4 or more.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.3 Redox suffixes
Redox suffixes are used to signify the degree to which a horizon is affected by reduction due to persistent waterlogging, as evidenced by both the matrix colour (Section 13.2) and the degree of development of redox segregations.
Redox segregations are formed as a result of the reduction and solubilisation of iron and/or manganese, their translocation and concentration, and their re-oxidation and precipitation in the form of oxides. They may comprise any of the following: redox mottles (Section 13.3), concentrations, coatings, and pans (Chapter 15).




Table 18.7: Redox suffixes

Name
Description

Slightly reduced
A horizon that contains more than 2% redox segregations, but no evidence of reduction. No low-chroma colours can be found in the matrix, on ped surfaces or in their interiors
B, C


(g)
Moderately reduced
A horizon that contains more than 2% redox segregations, and evidence of partial reduction. The matrix colour is not low-chroma, but low-chroma colours will be evident. These colours must occupy less than 50% of the cut face of a horizon, or less than 50% of ped surfaces
E, B, C


g
Strongly reduced
A horizon that contains more than 2% redox segregations, and evidence of extensive reduction. The matrix colour is low-chroma, and low-chroma colours occupy 50-85% of the cut face of a horizon, or over 50% of ped surfaces
A, E, B, C


r
Intensely reduced
A horizon that shows evidence of complete or near-complete reduction. The soil matrix comprises >85% low-chroma colours, either on the cut face of a horizon or on ped surfaces. Usually few to no redox segregations are present, and any that are will usually be confined to voids (e.g. in root channels).
E, B, C










Rule for use follow.

Only choose one redox suffix per horizon, if needed (e.g. Bg); the definitions are mutually exclusive.
g and r suffixes cannot be used with Ea, Ew or Bw horizons because they are partly defined by their development under well-aerated conditions and so will not have enough low-chroma colours in the matrix or on ped faces to qualify.
only the g suffix can be added to A horizons, in cases where ≥2% redox segregations occur. This is because A horizons are expected to be low-chroma from elevated organic matter, so do not meet the requirements for (f) or (g) suffixes. The use of the g suffix in A horizons may not necessarily signify strong reduction.

For further discussion about assessing redox intensity in soils, see Section 19.1. Table 18.8 summarises the colour and redox segregation requirements in Table 18.7 for quick reference.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.4 Additional suffixes
One or more of these suffixes can used to provide more specific information about a horizon. They are placed after any redox suffixes in use For example, a Bg horizon containing more than 5% by volume of concretions is designated Bgc.




Table 18.9: Additional suffixes















Code
Name
Description
Used with




c
Concretionary
To denote that the horizon contains >5% by volume of concretions - spherical bodies with concentric internal fabric. The suffix should be used in combination with other letters to indicate the nature of the concretionary material.
A, E, B, C


u
Fluid
A horizon that has a moderately or very fluid fluidity class.
A, E, B, C


(h)
Cutanic


A horizon with cutanic horizon properties. These horizons have dark-coloured coats on ped faces, in pores and on rock fragments.

A cutanic horizon meets both of the following criteria.

The coatings do not have a waxy lustre when dry or are not sufficiently thick to envelop fine sand grains. Silt coatings are excluded. (Silt coatings have similar colour to the matrix, or have a higher value and/or lower chroma than the matrix. On drying they may be thick enough to meet argillic horizon requirements, and have flow-like surfaces, but they have a matt rather than a waxy lustre.); and
The coatings have moist colour values of 4 or less, or value 5 and chroma 3 or less.

In coarse-textured, apedal horizons the translocated material can penetrate the matrix to the extent that patches of the whole horizon have the colour given above. In such cases the horizon can only be distinguished from a Bh of a podzolised soil by its relationship to adjacent horizons, or by a negative reaction to the sodium fluoride test, except for soil in volcaniclastic or pyroclastic materials.
The suffix is used with Bs, Bt, Bw and BC horizons and also with Ea, Eg and Er horizons below humose or peaty surface layers.
B, C


i
Nodular
Denotes that the horizon contains >5% by volume of nodules, subrounded or irregular segregations of iron or aluminium oxyhydroxides with some kaolin.
A, E, B, C


j
Jarositic
Denotes the presence of straw-coloured jarosite, most commonly in strongly or intensely reduced horizons.
A, E, B, C


k
Calcareous
Denotes an accumulation of fine-earth carbonate, CaCO3, usually detectable using field testing with HCl. The carbonate may be primary (inherited from soil parent materials) or secondary (precipitated from the soil solution). Coarse primary carbonate particles may or may not also be present but do not by themselves contribute to the definition of a calcareous horizon.
B, BC, C


l
Redox
To denote accumulation of >5% by volume iron-rich precipitated segregations (along with varying amounts of other redox-sensitive elements, notably manganese) sourced from groundwater aeration. The segregations may be soft or hard, and may or may not exhibit an internal structure. They form primarily on aggregate surfaces or along root channels in fine-textured soil materials, or throughout the interconnected void space in coarser soil materials.
A, E, B, C


m
Cemented
Denotes a continuously cemented horizon that is strong enough to resist root penetration. A continuously cemented horizon is one in which the primary mineral particles are chemically bound together by precipitated secondary minerals (e.g. silica, carbonate, metal oxides or ice). A cemented horizon is at least weakly indurated and has no (or no closely spaced) cracks, pores or soft spots that could allow root penetration. Where the agent cementing the horizon can be identified with confidence, the ‘m’ suffix is combined with the appropriate modifier (e.g. qm for a duripan).
B, BC, C


n
Sodic
Denotes a significant accumulation of exchangeable sodium. Sodic soil materials have an exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP) of ≥6% and an uncemented dry sample will exhibit moderate to complete dispersion. Natural sodicity is most common in B horizons.
B, BC, C


q
Silicic
Denotes an accumulation of secondary silica. Silica accumulations are cemented, pale, and do not react to 10% HCl. They may exist as nodules, patches, hard coatings, or most often as continuous pans, called duripans.
B, BC, C


v
Variegated
Denotes a horizon with mottles or variegated colour pattern due to differential weathering of mineral components and not attributable to reduction and segregation of iron caused by saturation with water.
BC, C


x
Fragipan


Denotes a non-cemented horizon that has high bulk density (usually ≥1.5 Mg/m3) with high strength when dry. A fragipan must fulfill all of the following requirements.


An air-dried sample slakes when fully immersed in water.
It has brittle failure when moist. The horizon may contain rock fragments, but the fine earth must be sufficiently coherent to allow brittle failure.
It has at least slightly firm unconfined soil strength when moist.
It has either a. prismatic peds with a size of >100 mm: the prisms have apedal-massive interiors, or break to secondary peds with horizontal dimensions of 100 mm or more, and the prism faces are defined by colours of chroma 3 or less, or b. a horizon that is apedal massive throughout, or has prismatic peds with a size of >100 mm, and the moist, unconfined soil strength is very firm.
If roots are present, they are predominantly confined to planar voids between prisms or to worm burrows.
Penetration resistance under moist conditions is 3,100 kPa or more.
It does not occur within an E horizon.

A fragipan usually has clay coatings on fissures or in pores between fissures, but an additional ‘t’ suffix is considered redundant where these are observed.
B, BC, C


(x)
Brittle
To denote a horizon that meets some but not all of the requirements of a fragipan; e.g. Bw(x).
B, BC, C


y

To denote an accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4).
B, BC, C


z
Salty
To denote an accumulation of salts more soluble than gypsum.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.5 Transitional horizons
Two main kinds of transitional horizons are distinguished by specific conventions.

Transitional horizons having properties of two master horizons, as in gradational horizons in vertical sequence (e.g. Ap-AB-Bw). In other cases a horizon can be designated as transitional even if one of the master horizons to which it is apparently transitional is not present. For example, an AB horizon can be recognised where the underlying layer is bedrock (R), and a BC horizon can be recognised even if no underlying C horizon is identified. Lower-case suffixes (see Section 18.3 and Section 18.4) are used following the two capital letters where the property denoted by the suffix applies to the whole horizon (e.g. ABg, BCt, BCx).
Transitional horizons in which discrete parts have recognisable properties of two kinds of master horizon (e.g. where pieces of A horizon are incorporated in a B horizon, or where horizons interfinger). In this case the horizon is designated by two capital letters separated by a solidus (e.g. B/C). Appropriate suffixes should be used where the components of the material are clearly identifiable (e.g. Ap/Bw).

For simplicity the capital letters for all transitional horizons are used in the order A, E, B, C, irrespective of which properties dominate. For example, all horizons transitional between A and B horizons are designated AB or A/B, with suffixes as appropriate.




Table 18.10: Common transitional horizons













Code
Description




A/B
A transitional horizon at the interface between the A and B horizons, where substantial biological mixing or dense, shrink–swell cracking has produced a horizon with distinct but intermingled zones of A and B horizon material. More than one-third of the material is clearly identifiable as originating from the overlying A horizon. The B horizon material may qualify as Bo, Bs, Bw or Bt and may or may not also have a redox suffix applied (e.g. Apg/Bg).


AB
A horizon transitional in character between an A and a B horizon, usually below an A horizon. It is distinguished from a B horizon by any or all of: having a darker colour due to relatively elevated organic matter, having less-developed structural units, and/or having a structure closer in character to the overlying A horizon. An AB horizon may also lack secondary features expressed lower in the B horizon, or show weaker development of the same.


BC
A horizon transitional in character between a B and a C horizon, usually below a B horizon. It is distinguished from a B horizon in similar material by lacking some required characteristic of colour, pedality or degree of weathering. It differs from a C horizon by having some B horizon feature, albeit weakly expressed. Note that a BC horizon can be identified in a profile without needing to first identify an overlying B (e.g. a horizon sequence of A-BC-C down-profile).


CR
A weakly consolidated C horizon that is sufficiently dense and coherent to form a significant barrier to roots. Soft rocks (with a hardness on Moh's scale of <3), such as shale and siltstone and some exceptionally dense glacial tills and pyroclastic deposits, are included. The material can be dug with difficulty with a spade when moist. The concept of the CR horizon is similar to that of the material underlying a paralithic contact, but without the restrictive requirement for the spacing of cracks.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.6 Numbering similar horizons
If multiple horizons with the same name but minor differences in morphology are evident in a profile, distinguish the horizons by appending them with a number, in the order in which they are encountered down the profile. The horizon names must otherwise be identical; for example, Bt1, Bt2, Btg1, Btg2 is correct, but Bt1, Bt2, Btg3, Btg4 is not. This convention can, however, cross lithological discontinuities (e.g. Bw1, Bw2, 2Bw3, 2Bw4). The convention can also be interrupted (e.g. Ah1, Bt, bAh2). The numerical suffix must always be placed last in the name.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.7 Lithological discontinuities
A numbered prefix may be used to group horizons within lithological or stratigraphic zones separated by discontinuities. Such discontinuities are identified by a significant difference between adjacent horizons in the particle-size distribution or in mineralogy, which cannot be attributed to pedogenic processes. The main purpose of recognising lithological differences is to draw attention to inherited layering that can significantly influence physical properties, particularly permeability, as well as providing insight into the landscape and land-use history that can be represented by a multilayered profile.
Horizons comprising the uppermost parent material layer are not specifically designated ‘1’, as many profiles contain no discontinuities and so the information would usually be superfluous. The subsequent layers are numbered 2, 3, etc. consecutively with depth, incrementing at each stratigraphic break. Each number may be applied to multiple adjacent horizons, until and unless another discontinuity is encountered. A change in parent material origin class (see Section 11.8.2) may often signify a discontinuity, but multiple discontinuities can exist within a sequence of the same parent material origin class, particularly in transported materials. Table 18.11 shows an example of correct usage of discontinuity prefixes in such a profile.

title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.8 Buried horizons
Pedogenic horizons that have been buried by the deposition of additional material and little modified subsequently are called buried horizons and denoted using the prefix ‘b’. A buried horizon is obviously not in the same deposit as overlying horizons. Some buried horizons, however, are formed in material that is lithologically similar to the overlying deposit. The symbol is not used in Organic Soils or to separate an organic layer from a mineral layer.
Buried soil horizons, even when only very weakly weathered, mark soil formation that took place through top-down processes when that parent material was at the land surface. They represent disconformities and carry information on landscape evolution, climate, and time. The boundary between the top of a buried soil and an overlying tephra or other geological deposit is a paraconformity, marking a period of non-deposition (Palmer et al. 2025).
The notation for a buried Ah horizon in material similar to the overlying deposit is bAh, and that for a buried Ah horizon in dissimilar material is 2bAh. The horizons of a sequence of buried soils are given consecutive numbers for each soil following the prefix b, independently of the numbers for lithological discontinuities that are placed before the b. title: 18  Horizon notation
text:
18.9 Anthropogenic horizons
Horizons formed in anthropogenic soil materials are denoted using the prefix ‘e’ (e.g. eAp). This may include deliberately manufactured soils (e.g. for sports fields or mine rehabilitation), or natural soils that have a significant component of anthropogenic modification (e.g. backyard soils, kūmara fields). The remaining horizons of a truncated profile should not receive this designation, nor should agricultural topsoils that have only been subject to low-impact and reversible practices like tillage or fertilisation.
Given that most anthropogenic soils in New Zealand will be less than about 800 years old, it is considered unlikely at present that the ‘e’ prefix will be valid when applied to subsoil horizons that require long periods of time to form (e.g. Bo).

title: 19  Profile behaviour
text:
19.1 Drainage
Soil profile descriptions can be used to identify behavioural characteristics of a soil that are relevant to ecosystem composition and agricultural productivity.
Soil drainage refers to the ability of water to move through the soil profile (internal drainage) as well as the amount of water the soil receives from surface or underground sources and how rapidly that water can leave (external drainage).
Internal drainage is partly determined by soil permeability (see Section 19.2), which in turn depends on structure, texture, and consistence. External drainage includes both drainage to greater depth or downslope and upward loss through evapotranspiration, so is determined by profile position in the landscape, adjacent soil and rock, the depth and nature of the subsolum, vegetation cover, and local climate. Land management practices will also affect the drainage regime.

title: 19  Profile behaviour
text:
19.1.1 Classifying drainage
The profile drainage classification defined in this handbook was originally developed for the New Zealand Soil Classification. The classes are relatively simple, based on the intensity of reduction observed within a given distance of the soil surface. Horizons are assessed for their reduction intensity using the rules in Table 19.1 (along with the guidance in Section 19.1.3 and Section 19.1.4), and then profile drainage is determined using Table 19.2.
For example: use MW for a soil profile with the sequence Ap (0-25 cm) over Bw(f) (25-45 cm) over B(g) (45-75 cm) over Bg (75-95 cm).

Note 19.1: Drainage classification and the New Zealand Soil Classification





In the New Zealand Soil Classification, *(f) or *(g) horizons (slightly to moderately anaerobic) qualify for the diagnostic ‘redox-mottled horizon’. Horizons with O*, *g, or *r notation (strongly to intensely anaerobic) qualify for the diagnostic ‘reductimorphic horizon’. However, *(f) horizons do not contribute to the ‘mottled profile form’ diagnostic.
It follows that only profiles with overall imperfect drainage are considered to have a ‘Mottled Profile Form’, and (non-peat) profiles with poor or very poor drainage have a ‘Gley Profile Form’.





19.1.2 Classifying perched profiles
Soil profiles sometimes exhibit perching behaviour, where a zone of more intense reduction in the subsoil exists directly above a low-permeability layer that appears to be less intensely reduced. These must be treated the same as any other soil profile when classifying. The depth to the shallowest zone of impeded drainage is used to determine the profile drainage class. Treat Table 19.2 as a key, stopping at the first class that fits the profile.
For example: use PO for a soil profile with the sequence Ap (0-15 cm) over Bg (15-35 cm) over B(g)x (35-65 cm) over BC(g)(x) (65-95 cm).


19.1.3 Assessing redox intensity in mineral topsoils
Morphological features associated with anaerobic conditions can be hard to observe accurately in mineral topsoils (A horizons). A horizons are usually darkened by organic matter accumulation and so may be low-chroma without necessarily being subject to reduction.
General principles for assessing the reduction intensity of an A horizon are as follows.

A horizons that are darkened but that do not have low-chroma matrix colours (e.g. 10YR 3/3  ) should be considered aerobic.
A horizons that do have a low-chroma matrix but otherwise meet the criteria for ‘distinct topsoils’ in the New Zealand Soil Classification (i.e. visibly darker than the subsoil and at least 5 cm thick) should be considered to be subject to less intense reduction than the horizon immediately underneath. For example, a 15 cm thick Ap horizon with moderate structure over a Bw(f) horizon would be considered aerobic, while an Ap immediately over a B(g) would be considered slightly anaerobic. The degree of underlying reduction in the latter case suggests that some limited periods of wetness should occur in the topsoil.
Other weakly developed or very thin A horizons should usually be considered to have the same degree of redox intensity as the horizon below.
Apg horizons, with their identifiable redox segregations, must be considered to be moderately anaerobic under the majority of circumstances.
If an Apg horizon has a slightly peaty texture with weak or massive apedal structure, or clearly identifiable gley colour patterns, it can be considered strongly anaerobic.

Some caution should be exercised when assessing topsoils in agricultural landscapes. In some cases, topsoil redox segregations form in response to surface compaction from stock pugging, vehicle traffic, or tillage under wet conditions, while the deeper profile remains relatively unaffected. Clear description of the soil surface (Chapter 10) will help prevent the presence of an Apg horizon from inappropriately downgrading profile drainage in this situation.


19.1.4 Assessing redox intensity in mixed transitional horizons
For transitional A/B horizons, if the A horizon component is sub-dominant by volume, then it should simply be ignored for the assessment of redox intensity.
For example: in an A/B horizon where earthworm activity has moved dark A horizon material down through vertical burrows that occupy about 25% of the cut face of the soil horizon, the infilled burrows should not contribute to the total percentage of low-chroma colours in the soil matrix. The horizon would be assessed as if it were an unmixed B.
Where the A horizon material occupies the majority of the transitional zone, it can no longer be ignored. The topsoil component of the horizon should be assessed using the instructions in Section 19.1.3, but the subsoil component of the horizon sets a lower limit on reduction intensity.
For example: in an Ap/B(g) horizon where tillage has partially mixed the topsoil and subsoil, the transition zone can be considered slightly anaerobic.


19.1.5 Assessing redox intensity in low-chroma parent materials
Exercise caution when assigning redox suffixes to soil horizons dominated by mafic/intermediate parent materials (e.g. basalt andesite, see Section 4.2) because their colour usually appears darker than that of felsic parent materials (i.e. low chroma and low value) due to their mineralogy. Consequently, low-chroma colours appear less distinct.
Other soil parent materials can have low-chroma colours when relatively unweathered, e.g. young pumice deposits, unweathered greywacke sands, and marine-deposited sedimentary rocks. Heavily leached soil horizons (e.g. E horizons) will often be both high-value and low-chroma. Distinguishing the influence of drainage in these materials requires examining them under a range of drainage conditions, to better understand their natural variability.
As well as becoming familiar with the range of parent material appearance, using field tests for reducing conditions (Section 17.6) can help increase the accuracy of horizon notation provided sufficient free iron (Fe2+) remains in the soil solution.


19.1.6 Natural vs artificial drainage
Profile drainage is often modified by human activity, and many of these modifications require ongoing maintenance. Use a code from Table 19.3 to indicate the degree of drainage modification.
For example, use IP A for a profile on low-lying plain that is located adjacent to a deep artificial drain.




Table 19.3: Profile drainage modification level














Code
Name
Description




N
Natural
No evidence of human impacts on the local drainage regime


M
Minor
Drainage regime passively altered (e.g. by conversion to or from forest), or ambiguous evidence of any human impacts beyond clearing


A
Major
Clear evidence of directed human alteration to the drainage regime (e.g. drain or dam construction adjacent to site, flow diversions, infill, levelling or contouring works)












19.1.7 Within-class drainage variability
Users of this handbook may sometimes wish to distinguish between soil profiles that have the same profile drainage class but a variable expression of reduction depth and intensity within the class limits. For example, for a deep-rooted, wetness-intolerant crop, there is a difference between an imperfectly drained profile that is at its worst moderately reduced throughout the top 90 cm, and one that has strong or intense reduction at depth.
Within-class distinctions can be highlighted by appending the most intense reduction class observed within the profile.
For example, use IP(v) for an imperfectly drained profile with intense reduction deep in the profile, vs IP(i) for an imperfectly drained profile where the reduction intensity does not exceed moderate.

title: 19  Profile behaviour
text:
19.2 Permeability
Permeability is the measured or estimated rate at which water moves through the soil under ‘free-draining’ conditions (i.e. in the absence of barriers and in an unsaturated state). Permeability is assessed first on a per-horizon basis before the profile as a whole is summarised.
Permeability can be measured directly, and while these data are always preferred, the measurement process is time-consuming and labour intensive. As a result, a great deal of research effort has been directed towards developing reliable estimates of permeability for New Zealand soils based on soil morphology (McLaughlin and Watt 1989; Griffiths 1991; Webb and Lilburne 2011). This section describes a method of permeability estimation based on that work.

19.2.1 Horizon permeability
For each horizon, in the absence of direct measurements use texture group, structure, stone content, organic matter content, and unconfined strength at field condition to rate permeability using the characteristics described in Table 19.4.
Note that for each permeability class, topsoil horizons and soils with tephric parent materials are generally considered to be one class more permeable than described (e.g. a clayey topsoil horizon with <20 mm peds would be assigned moderate rather than moderately slow permeability).

title: 19  Profile behaviour
text:
19.3 Rooting depth restrictions
Some soils contain barriers to plant root growth that can affect some or all species, depending on the natural size of their root systems and their tolerance for particular conditions. Such barriers can include physical properties (soil firmness, buried rock or concrete), chemical properties (pH, salinity, macro- and micro-nutrient levels, presence of pollutants), biological properties (pathogens, pests), and hydrological properties (excessive wetness or dryness).
Rooting depth barriers can be identified most clearly by the behaviour of living roots in the profile. Absence of roots beyond a certain depth where vegetation is present at the surface may indicate a barrier, assuming the species present normally have a deep-rooting growth habit. Roots may also be observed to grow downwards until encountering a barrier and then turn to grow horizontally, sometimes forming subsurface mats. Root density may decrease suddenly at a horizon boundary without disappearing entirely, perhaps becoming sparse and confined to voids. Significant barriers may also affect the character of vegetation at the surface, causing for example, stunted growth.
Where rooting behaviour appears to be impaired, evidence of a likely cause can be inferred from the profile description, particularly:

field tests for pH, salinity or reducing conditions (Chapter 17)
strength, penetration resistance and induration tests (Chapter 16)
structural characteristics, particularly the absence of peds or inter-ped spaces (Section 12.1)
relative abundance of rock fragments, where excess rock might be a physical barrier and also limit water retention and movement (Section 12.2)
soil texture, where high clay content may cause waterlogging or high sand content may limit water retention (Chapter 14)
identification of pans blocking root growth, or concentrations that may suggest a chemical issue (Chapter 15).

Where these features are observed, in order to be considered as a potential rooting depth barrier their occurrence must usually coincide with the zone where root behaviour changes or roots disappear. Only a few barriers (e.g. bedrock) can be considered definite regardless of whether any roots are actually present in the profile. Where no obvious restricting features are present but impeded root growth is still observable, laboratory testing may be required to investigate the cause.
Record rooting barrier information as type using Table 19.6 and depth encountered in cm.
For example: use Bm 30 cm for a shallow profile over bedrock.
Rooting depths should usually coincide with a horizon boundary.




Table 19.6: Types of rooting barrier














Code
Name
Description

Ak

Na

Ax

Tx
Toxic

Nx

Fm

Pp

Bm

Note 19.2: Biological impedances to root growth





Biological soil features may act as restrictions on plant root growth. Examples include pathogens, root-eating pest species, and allelopathic pressures from other plant species and/or soil organisms. These are not presently included in the list of root barriers in Table 19.6, for several reasons:

the ability to reliably identify these factors during field soil survey is currently limited
where present, these factors are more likely to be a whole-of-profile feature than one that appears at a particular depth
these factors may only affect certain species or genera.

Nonetheless, if a biological root growth impedance is known to occur at a location where a soil profile is being described, it should be recorded as a free-text note. Samples taken from the profile may require careful handling (e.g. to avoid spreading a pathogen), and field equipment and clothing may require decontamination.

title: Appendix A — Equipment
text: A.1 Profile exposure tools

title: Appendix A — Equipment
text:
A.1.1 Hand
Excavation by hand is often the only viable option in New Zealand terrain, with often severely limited vehicle access. A heavy-duty steel spade with a wooden handle is the default choice. Other options that might suit particular environments include long-handled fencing spades and narrow trenching shovels. A breaker bar or crowbar may also be needed to loosen the soil before excavating.
Hand augers are common tools for rapid profile extraction, but with the exception of gouge augers for soft muds the degree to which they disturb the soil profile means they are better off as an accessory tool. Augering is best confined to well-understood landscapes where quick cores are used to confirm that observations made in nearby pits are representative of the area being sampled.
Auger heads useful for soil observations include

50–100 mm heads for loamy to light clayey soils
30–50 mm heads for lightly gravelly soils
open-ended heads for augering in sands and fine gravels
gouge augers for sampling soft muds.

Extendable systems are useful for reaching target depths of >1 m, and systems with shorter rods may offer a better ergonomic experience for shorter workers. Augering safely and efficiently becomes difficult when the handles are above the base of the user’s ribcage.
C2 (Table 9.3) style tube samplers can be manually inserted with a steel post-driver and sampling depths of up to 1 m are usually achievable.


A.1.2 Mechanical
Mechanical post-drivers can be adapted to push C2 sampling tubes in as deep as 1.5 m, provided the substrate is minimally stony and soil moisture conditions are favourable. Sampling in 30–50 cm sections may be necessary in some cases.






Figure A.1: A researcher using a post-driver to extract a C1 style core in the upper Rangitikei River valley.



Sampling in gravelly, dry-clayey or hard-setting soils may not be feasible without the use of an excavator. Compact models that can be moved on a light trailer are preferred. A narrow bucket gives the operator a choice of pit sizes.






Figure A.2: A pedologist is seen operating a small mechanical excavator to open up a P1 sampling pit on an alluvial plain in Northland.



For deeper sampling, or work in saturated soils, consider the use of vehicle-mounted dual tube sampling systems, where a C1 core is lined with a removable plastic tube. These are usually pushed into the soil with a hydraulic hammer and the more complex systems can sample to well over 10 m. Another option is vacuum-assisted coring for working below the water-table.
Mechanical screw augers are not recommended because they disturb the soil profile too much for a reliable description. Hollow-core screw augers, however, may be able to minimise such disturbance.

title: Appendix A — Equipment
text:
A.2 Peat sampling
Sampling peats can be challenging due to their flexible structure and high water content. Advice on peat-specific extraction devices can be found in Dettmann et al. (2022) and Agus et al. (2011).

title: Appendix A — Equipment
text:
A.3 Profile description tools
Essential small tools for a field sampling kit include:

pit tape with large markings, 1–5 m length
1–3 m measuring tape
Munsell colour book
putty knife or trowel (plus a plastic option for sampling reduced horizons)
spray bottle or pressure sprayer for water
nails, golf tees or small marker flags for noting horizon boundaries (and pinning the pit tape into place)
cleaning cloths
notepad and pen, or electronic field recording device
camera
GPS receiver
batteries and/or power packs, and charging cables for electronics
clinometer
compass
plastic sample bags
permanent markers
tarpaulin or mat for laying out excavated profiles (a minimum 100 mm diameter polyethylene half-pipe or flat wooden board may also be used for auger samples).

A smartphone or similar device can be substituted for much of the data recording and sensing equipment listed above but users should check water- and dust-proofing, battery life, screen brightness, image quality, sensor accuracy and ergonomics before field use. Cameras (see Section B.3) and location-sensing capabilities especially are highly variable between devices.
Optional, but useful, tools include:

rock hammer
small sieve with 2 mm mesh for removing coarse rock fragments before texturing
sand-grade sieves for separating sand fraction subdivisions
gardening clippers for trimming overhanging vegetation around exposures
medium-bristled brush, for cleaning up exposure faces
small whiteboard and markers for noting site identifiers in profile photographs
extendable snap-blade knife for precise sample excision in moist soils
Niwashi gardening tool, for cleaning up pit faces and exposures
plastic frame with internal area of 100 cm2 for root count assessment (or to delineate an area with nails and twine).

A complete field kit should fit in a medium-sized toolbox or sturdy backpack.

title: Appendix A — Equipment
text:
A.4 Field test equipment
A portable field test kit should be contained in a waterproof storage box in case of reagent leaks. Kit contents may include any or all of the following, per Chapter 17:

Raupach field pH kit (Section 17.1.1)
10% or 1 M HCl (Section 17.3)
3–6% H2O2 (Section 17.4)
1 M NaF and pre-treated filter paper (Section 17.5).







Figure A.3: A photo of an open multi-compartment storage box containing field test kit reagents in small dropper bottles. The box is roughly 20 by 35 cm.



Portable electronic meters (e.g. for pH or EC) should travel in their own containers, along with calibration and cleaning equipment, as well as sample containers and a rack to hold them (Section 17.1.2, Section 17.1.3, and Section 17.2). A small toolbox will usually suffice.

title: Appendix B — Recording data in the field
text:
B.1 Data entry forms
Recording field data in a regularised format helps ensure that consistently high standards are kept. Well-structured and complete soil profile descriptions are key supports for subsequent analytical work, including mapping tasks and analysis of laboratory data.
Using a data entry form reduces the chance of forgetting to record particular data points, vs freehand notes. The consistent layout also makes it easier to review data for completeness and correctness, and to compare sites.
Data entry forms should be laid out so that the process of filling them out roughly follows the process of field soil description itself. Each section should contain enough room for the parameter being recorded. A high-detail, hard-copy field sheet should still fit on a single A4 page, despite the large number of potential parameters.
Forms can be deployed on paper, but they are vulnerable to wind and rain. Note-taking software on touchscreen tablets (e.g. Microsoft OneNote) can offer a robust alternative.
crumbs: B  Recording data in the field

title: Appendix B — Recording data in the field
text:
B.2 App-based data entry
Using a purpose-built app for data entry can reduce the double handling inherent in recording hard-copy data, freeing up office time. Apps do come with design, deployment, and maintenance overheads that need to be taken into account, as well as a significant learning curve for paper-adapted users. Graphical user interfaces, despite their huge potential, are currently (at the time of writing) surprisingly restrictive about layout and input options, and will generally take up more virtual ‘page space’ than a hard-copy sheet.
At the time of writing there is no consumer-grade app dedicated to recording New Zealand soils field data, but the ESRI and QGIS spatial software ecosystems have field data entry frameworks that can be adapted for soils fieldwork.
crumbs: B  Recording data in the field

title: Appendix B — Recording data in the field
text:
B.3 Taking and managing photographs
Site photographs provide a valuable record of the profile itself and the nature of the landscape in which it occurs. Photographs should include at least the following:

one to four landscape shots from different angles, placing the site in context: stand well back and, where possible, slightly uphill; try to capture reliable landmarks in the background and remove any extraneous objects (e.g. field equipment) that might be distracting
one clear photo of the ground condition around the profile, including a clearly marked measuring tape or stick for scale
one clear photo of the extracted profile or exposure with a measuring tape for scale: ideally take this photo after tidying the profile but before describing, so that it can be viewed in a minimally disturbed state
three to four close-up photos of the profile, capturing 30–40 cm depth ranges; these should slightly overlap.

Consider using a small whiteboard to include the site identifier and date in at least the profile photo. Any further photos (e.g. of concretions or other pedologically important soil features) are optional.
Profile photographs should be taken in clear sunlight with the light behind the photographer, or in full shade. Avoid dappled or dim light, or angled shadows. Note that high-visibility clothing can sometimes reflect light onto profiles in a way that distorts colour.
Using a dedicated field data recording app to take photographs can ensure they are always associated with the correct site identifier. Otherwise, photos should be organised on a per profile basis as soon as possible after fieldwork. The quickest method is simply to place them in a folder named after the site identifier. Renaming image files and/or adding subject-matter tags can be useful for longer-term storage, but the process can be time-consuming.

B.3.1 Photographic equipment
Most users will default to their smartphone camera. This is usually safe, but some newer models default to enhancing photos in ways that are optimised for recreational use rather than scientific data recording. Users should make an effort to understand how their devices are processing photographs and disable any features that may alter the images too heavily.
crumbs: B  Recording data in the field

title: Appendix B — Recording data in the field
text:
B.4 Minimum data requirements
Data recording requirements for classifying the profile against the New Zealand Soil Classification are available in Chapter 20, and data needed for some other systems are provided in Appendix E. In Table B.1 the minimum rapid, routine, and detailed recording options described throughout the main text are summarised. Note that there is no reason not to record particular parameters in more detail than the minimum if they are of interest.
Rapid descriptions are primarily made to confirm soil type in a landscape that is already well understood, or to support research work that is not focused on soil processes. Rapid descriptions are also appropriate for students learning soil description for the first time. Routine descriptions are preferred for most soil description work, particularly in the exploratory phases of mapping. Detailed dscriptions are preferred for soil-process-focused research work and for establishing ‘reference sites’ representative of common soil profiles in a region.
